question.leadin: The man who assassinated this president bought an ivory-handled revolver for it because he thought it would look better in a museum.
question.text: Name this president who was shot by Charles Guiteau, a man who was bitter about not receiving a lucrative government job.
question.clue: This man defeated Winfield Scott Hancock to become president, and the Pendleton Civil Service Act was passed after his death.

swap.leadin: Answer some questions about a famous American businessman who first became wealthy running a steamboat company.
swap.text: This man, nicknamed "commodore," was awarded a Congressional Gold Medal for the donation of his namesake steamship to the Union Navy.
swap.clue: During the California Gold Rush, this person created the Accessory Transit Company to bring passengers from the East Coast to San Francisco via Nicaragua.

question.text: This suffragette worked closely with Elizabeth Cady Stanton in fighting for the right to vote. She was the first woman to be portrayed on an American coin.
question.clue: This woman is the alleged author of "Marriage and Maternity," an article published in The Revolution.

swap.leadin: Give the following about Native Americans in the United States.
swap.text: This law attempted to eliminate the Native American "communal" way of living by dividing tribal land into allotments of 160 acres for families and 80 acres for individuals.
swap.clue: This 1887 act allowed the U.S. government to survey Indian tribal lands and divide them up among the individuals in the tribe to assimilate Indians into American society.

question.text: Before becoming mayor, La Guardia joined Moses in the Fusion Party to challenge this New York political machine once led by Boss Tweed.
question.clue: William Mooney was the first Grand Sachem of this group, that helped Al Smith secure the presidential nomination in 1928.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about labor movements in the U.S.
swap.text: This strike pitted the Amalgated Association of Iron and Steel Workers against the Carnegie Steel Company. Henry Clay Frick enlisted Pinkertons to break it up.
swap.clue: The leader of the Amalgamated Associations, Hugh O'Donnell, led this strike.

question.text: The Knights of Labor took a huge hit after this 1886 Chicago strike of workers because the AFL was soon founded after its occurence. It began after one demonstrator threw a bomb at an officer.
question.clue: Governor John Altgeld pardoned three men convicted of conspiracy for inciting this event.

swap.text: Note to Moderator: Be generous on pronunciation. While Robert Todd Lincoln was outside the Temple of Music at the 1901 Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo, New York, this anarchist shot William McKinley.
swap.clue: This immigrant, a disciple of the anarchist Emma Goldman, traveled to Buffalo and shot William McKinley in a reception line at the 1901 Pan-American Exposition.

question.text: After fighting against the Mexican government, he led a revolt on the San Carlos reservation against George Crook and surrendered to dishonest terms at Skeleton Canyon.
question.clue: This leader's name was used to signal the success of Operation Neptune Spear, in which Osama Bin Laden was killed, and George Crook lost his command after this man escaped.

swap.leadin: During the Civil War he led the Michigan Brigade, which was sometimes known as his "wolverines."
swap.text: Name this American general who followed up a victory over Black Kettle at Washita River with a crushing defeat at the hands of the Sioux at Little Big Horn.
swap.clue: The Battle of the Rosebud prevented George Crook from joining up with this man, who was killed by the forces of Sitting Bull.

question.text: In Elk Grove Unified School District v. Newdow, the Ninth Circuit said that the words "under God" in this statement violated the Establishment clause. The Supreme Court reversed the Ninth circuit's decision, but has also ruled that students do not need to salute the flag during this statement.
question.clue: In 1943, Jehovah's Witnesses argued that engaging in this practice constituted veneration in the landmark case West Virginia vs. Barnette.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about famous political cartoons from the 19th century.
swap.text: This Republican presidential candidate in 1884 was depicted in a cartoon as a "tattooed man," marred with numerous scandals. The Mugwumps refused to support this man, a former Secretary of State, in the 1884 election.
swap.clue: Bonds for the Little Rock and Fort Smith Railroad were the subject of this man's correspondence in the Mulligan Letters.

question.text: In response to the later decision Wabash v. Illinois that restricted states' authority to regulate railroads, Congress established this first independent regulatory agency.
question.clue: This organization had its power strengthened by the Hepburn and Mann Elkins Act, which regulated "unfair trade practices".

swap.leadin: Name some guys who have served as governor of New York in the 19th century.
swap.text: This Governor of New York also served as Secretary of State and helped resolve the dispute over the Alabama Claims, along with helping his President attempt to annex the Dominican Republic.
swap.clue: This name was held by a cabinet official who organized a plan to annex the Dominican Republic that was torpedoed by Charles Sumner.

question.leadin: Public outrage over this practice in New York City led to a 1788 riot during which John Jay was reportedly hit over the head with a rock.
question.text: Name this practice that inspired the passage of "bone bills" in several states, as introduced by the president of the American Chemical Society, John William Draper.
question.answerHtml: body snatching [accept equivalents like stealing corpses or digging up bodies; or cadaver research; prompt on grave robbing or stealing by asking “what objects were stolen?”]

swap.leadin: A Louisiana monopoly controlling these places was sued for limiting an asserted right to work.
swap.text: In a case named for these places, Associate Justice Samuel Miller ruled that the Privileges and Immunities Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment applied only to federal citizenship and not the states.
swap.answerHtml: slaughterhouses [accept meatpacking or meat processing factories or facilities; do not accept or prompt on “factories”]
swap.clue: This businesses that named a series of cases ruling that the Privileges and Immunities Clause protected only federal citizens.

question.text: The Weather Bureau lost credence with the American public after failing to foresee this 1900 disaster that killed around eight thousand people and devastated a city known as the "Wall Street of the Southwest."
question.answerHtml: Galveston Hurricane [or Galveston Flood; or 1900 Galveston Hurricane; prompt on Great Storm of 1900]
question.clue: This 1900 natural disaster, a Category 4 storm that killed between six and twelve thousand people and is still the deadliest single-day event in US history.

swap.leadin: According to lore, this event began when one participant mocked and humiliated the other for putting a skull on the wrong end of an Elasmosaurus skeleton.
swap.text: Name this late 19th century rivalry between two U.S. paleontologists, to see who could discover more dinosaurs in the American west.
swap.clue: That figure made further gains in this event by sending Samuel Williston to respond to a letter from two Union Pacific employees, thus gaining a huge foothold in Como Bluff.

question.text: Identifying "democratic" and "legislative" types of government, this speech given in Chicago at the DNC of 1896 ends with the speaker claiming "you shall not crucify mankind" on the title object.

swap.text: This man served as Garfield's secretary of state. He was later defeated in his own bid for the presidency in the election of 1884 by Grover Cleveland, and was fondly known as the "Continental Liar from the State of Maine."
swap.clue: He tried to mollify the American response to the USS Baltimore incident using contacts he made as chair of the first Pan-American Conference.
